objections.target: la_two_wheel_delivery_share (0.46 base) and two_wheel_delivery_to_courier_share (0.88): DoorDash's 49% is declared dash-type, not observed mode
objections.claim: DoorDash's 'percent of deliveries on two wheels' is the Dasher's self-selected dash type. In LA, where essentially every courier owns a car and DTLA/Koreatown are precisely the zones where 'bike' mode unlocks short, dense, high-paying orders that car mode never sees, a material share of 'two-wheel' deliveries are done from a car in bike/e-bike mode. The 49% is therefore an upper bound on real two-wheel activity, and the model haircuts it only for Uber Eats blending, not for mode misreporting.
objections.evidence: TikTok @bowtieguy_delivers (video 7327861501174271275): 'How to get short distance good paying orders on doordash by using the ebike function instead of dash with car'; TikTok discover pages 'How to put e bike mode on doordash' / 'How to change doordash directions to bike'. DoorDash's own policy text: 'Failing to accurately identify the mode of transportation being used to perform dashes is grounds for deactivation and will be monitored' (entrecourier.com bike-delivery guide, quoting DoorDash) - a rule that exists because the practice is common. Internal consistency check: if 'Los Angeles, CA' is the city and the 38.3M two-month miles (628k/day) were really ridden at 60 mi/day, DoorDash alone would have ~10,500 two-wheel daily-active couriers in the City of LA - more than the model's entire city all-mode daily-active count (10,005). A 60-mile 'bike' day is trivial in a car, hard on an e-bike. NYC DCWP already documents mode misreporting on the same platforms (mopeds self-reporting as e-bike).
objections.suggested_value_or_fix: Haircut the DoorDash 49% by 15-25% for car-in-bike-mode -> true DoorDash two-wheel delivery share 37-42%. Blend with Uber Eats LA (~20-30% two-wheel; Uber Eats + Postmates is stronger in LA than nationally, ~35% of orders, and draws from the rideshare car pool) and Grubhub -> ~35% all-app two-wheel deliveries. Courier factor 0.80 (NYC is 0.72; LA two-wheelers are the committed segment, car Dashers the casual majority) -> LA-wide two-wheel courier share ~0.28-0.30, not 0.40.
objections.effect_on_output: two_wheel_courier_share_la 0.40 -> ~0.29; feeds zone share down from 0.53 to ~0.40-0.42 even with a 1.4x core uplift; DAILY_zone_two_wheel ~1,000 -> ~750-850.

objections.target: zone_two_wheel_uplift (1.3x) -> two_wheel_courier_share_zone 0.53: who actually delivers in each sub-zone
objections.claim: A single 1.3x uplift on an LA-wide figure ignores that the five sub-zones have very different courier pools. Restaurant-weighted, the zone's two-wheel COURIER share is ~40-43%, not 53%.
objections.evidence: Restaurant-weighted sub-zone estimate from ground observation patterns: DTLA (910 restaurants, 46% weight) ~50% two-wheel couriers (7th/Fig, Grand Central Market, Little Tokyo have visible e-bike/standing-scooter riders; parking friction is real); Koreatown (611, 31%) ~35% (6th/Western/Olympic at 7pm is dominated by double-parked cars with hazards on; late-night volume is car-heavy; Latino riders on gas mopeds/e-bikes are present but a minority); Westlake+Pico-Union (230, 12%) ~45% (41.8% / 25.6% zero-vehicle households, short hops); USC (211, 11%) ~30% (car couriers from South LA serving Figueroa/Jefferson chains, plus Coco robots). Weighted: 0.46x50 + 0.31x35 + 0.12x45 + 0.11x30 = 42.6%. Korean-community sources ('우버이츠 도어대시 차로 배달 할만한 지역' on heykorean) describe Korean side-hustlers by car; they are a minority of the Ktown courier pool (Koreatown is ~53% Latino / ~30% Asian) but the car-majority observation at KBBQ pickups holds regardless of ethnicity. Note this is courier share; delivery share would sit ~8-10 points higher because two-wheelers do more drops/hour.
objections.suggested_value_or_fix: two_wheel_courier_share_zone lo 0.32 / base 0.42 / hi 0.50 (replace the uplift multiplier with an explicit sub-zone table so DTLA and Koreatown are not forced to the same number).
objections.effect_on_output: DAILY_zone_two_wheel base 1,000-1,040 -> ~750-800 (before the all-modes haircut); DAILY_zone_car rises correspondingly to ~1,050.

objections.claim: The 65% electric share is imported from NYC and does not survive LA conditions: it carries NYC's 24% rental e-bike segment (no LA equivalent), NYC's Fly-E-style e-bike retail ecosystem (absent in Koreatown), and NYPD moped seizures (no LA analogue). LA's structural drivers push gas 49cc/150cc scooters to ~30-35% of two-wheelers, and LA's 'electric' two-wheelers skew to standing e-scooters and sub-$1,200 fat-tire e-bikes, not e-mopeds.
objections.evidence: (1) Uber Eats LA's only motorized mode is 'scooter <50cc, 19+, driver's license' (uber.com/us/en/e/deliver/los-angeles-ca-us); a 49cc gas scooter needs only a Class C license (available to undocumented residents via AB 60), no M1, no registration hassle, no charging - and costs $899 new (2026 Keeway Shiny 50, Van Nuys dealer, multiple units in the Craigslist snapshot) vs $2,800 for a used NIU MQi GT; 50-150cc listings $899-2,795 (55 listings, 2026-09-06). (2) California is the only state where lane-splitting is legal, so a 125-150cc scooter beats a car on Wilshire/Olympic/Figueroa while a Class 2 e-bike is capped at 20 mph on 35-45 mph arterials with 2-5 mile legs (ShiftTracker LA leg lengths). (3) Westlake/Pico-Union pre-war walk-ups without garages: a 1-2 kWh e-bike battery goes upstairs, a 25-30 kg e-moped pack does not; gas needs no plug. (4) Direct DTLA artefact: YouTube 'Honda Ruckus Scooter/Moped Food Delivery Set-up with Links - DoorDash UberEats Downtown Los Angeles'. (5) Supply side for electric skews standing-scooter: Levy Electric partner shops at 4001 Wilshire Blvd (90010), 2277 W Pico Blvd (90006), 3008 & 109 Vermont Ave; only gas dealer surfaced is L A SCOOTERS, 11316 S Vermont (South LA). No e-moped dealer or battery-swap network in the zone. (6) Whizz lists 6 US markets, LA excluded; Zoomo's US site now titles every page 'Zoomo NYC' and its 'Zoomo Los Angeles' Facebook page is a relic - the rental-e-bike segment (24% of NYC's intercept sample) is ~0% in LA. (7) LA's Latino courier base comes from moto-delivery cultures (Mexico/Central America/Colombia/Venezuela: 125-150cc motos on Rappi/Didi).
objections.suggested_value_or_fix: Split the two-wheel fleet as: gas scooter/motorcycle 0.30-0.35; standing e-scooter 0.12-0.15 (new bucket - not an HMP e-moped upgrade customer in the same way); e-bike incl. e-moto (Surron/Talaria, Super73/Ariel) 0.35-0.40; e-moped proper (NIU/Segway/HMP-class) 0.03-0.05; pedal 0.08-0.10. 'e-bike/e-moped' ex standing scooters = ~0.42 of two-wheel.
objections.effect_on_output: DAILY_zone_ebike_emoped ~650 -> ~320-360 (excluding standing e-scooters) or ~430-460 (including them). Combined with objections 1-2 the correction is ~0.5x.

objections.target: weekly_to_daily_active (0.4) applied to two-wheel couriers -> TAM_people_zone_two_wheel 2,528 and everything downstream
objections.claim: The blended 0.4 daily/weekly ratio describes casual car Dashers (DoorDash CA average ~6 hrs/week). Two-wheel couriers are the committed segment - they bought a vehicle for the job - and work 5-6 days a week. Dividing the two-wheel daily count by 0.4 assumes the average two-wheel courier works 2.8 days/week and inflates the two-wheel 'people' pool by ~1.7x.
objections.evidence: Model arithmetic: BLEND_zone_two_wheel_weekly_people 2,528 = BLEND_zone_two_wheel_daily 1,011 / 0.4. NYC DCWP: non-car couriers 22.2 hrs/wk vs car 17.5; NYC full-timers 6+ days/wk (daily/weekly ~0.85 per the model's own note). Berkeley 2024: 59% of CA delivery trips by 20+ hr/wk drivers - the two-wheel fleet lives inside that minority. In LA the casual after-work Dasher uses the car already in the driveway; nobody buys a $900 gas scooter or $1,500 e-bike to dash two evenings a week.
objections.suggested_value_or_fix: Use a mode-specific ratio: two-wheel daily/weekly 0.65-0.75 (base 0.7); keep 0.35-0.4 for car couriers. Weekly two-wheel people = ~750-800 daily / 0.7 = ~1,100-1,150.
objections.effect_on_output: TAM_people_zone_two_wheel 2,528 -> ~1,100-1,200 (-55%); SAM_people_hub 1,009 -> ~400-500 before the reachability objection; SOM scales proportionally.

objections.target: county_share_of_doordash_label_miles (0.9) and the M5 miles route / nyc_miles_calibration (0.6)
objections.claim: The DoorDash label is almost certainly a city-scale submarket, not the metro, and under that reading M5 does not corroborate M1-M3 - it contradicts them by ~2x. The blend therefore presents false agreement between routes.
objections.evidence: Label granularity: the same table lists Santa Clara (7.7M mi), Sunnyvale (6.9M), San Jose (28.4M), Oakland (10.0M) and San Francisco (21.4M) as separate 'cities' - a metro convention would never separate Sunnyvale from San Jose. DoorDash's Dash Report uses 'Greater Los Angeles' when it means the metro; the two-wheel table says 'Los Angeles, CA'. Under a city label: 9,419 label two-wheel daily-actives x 17.2% (zone share of city restaurants) x 1.3 = ~2,100 zone two-wheel daily, 2.1x the model's 981; and 9,419 DoorDash-only two-wheel riders would exceed the model's 4,050 city two-wheel and approach its 10,005 city all-mode total. The 0.6 NYC calibration that pulls M5 down was derived assuming DoorDash holds 28% of NYC (2022 McKinsey figure); DoorDash's NYC share has grown substantially since, so the 'overshoot' may be an artefact of a stale share, not evidence about the miles metric. Either the miles are padded (car-in-bike-mode, objection 1) or LA has far more couriers than M1-M3 say; M5 cannot tell you which.
objections.suggested_value_or_fix: Remove M5 from the blend or report it as an unresolved range (zone two-wheel 700 under metro reading to 2,100 under city reading) with no base; set county_share_of_doordash_label_miles to 'undefined' rather than 0.9. Ask DoorDash press/policy for the label boundary and whether 'miles traveled' includes miles logged while online without an active delivery.
objections.effect_on_output: BLEND_zone_two_wheel_daily loses its second leg; the M5-vs-M123 agreement ratio 0.94 should not be cited as validation. Direction of net effect is indeterminate, which is itself the point.

objections.claim: 768 Ceres Ave is an 8,443 sf industrial box with one loading dock, climate control and zero retail frontage in the Produce/Warehouse District at the southern lip of Skid Row (7th St). It has no walk-in discovery, is unsafe-feeling for a rider with a $3-5k vehicle after dark, and is 4+ road miles from the zone's densest restaurant cluster. 0.5 is a one-time-sale number; for anything involving repeat visits (battery swap, rental, service) it is 0.35-0.4.
objections.evidence: LoopNet/PropertyShark listing: built 2015, 8,443 sf, 1 loading dock, '10 Freeway @ Central Ave', asking $1.20/sf/mo industrial - i.e., not a storefront. Road distances from 34.0363,-118.2447: 7th/Figueroa ~1.5 mi; Alvarado/6th (Westlake) ~2.8 mi; Figueroa/Jefferson (USC) ~2.7 mi; Wilshire/Western (Koreatown core, 31% of zone restaurants) ~4.5 mi, i.e., 20-25 min each way by e-moped through DTLA and past Skid Row. HMP's SF traction came from a founder-staffed walk-in store in a 47 sq mi city; nothing walks past 768 Ceres except produce trucks and forklifts at 4am. Mitigant the model misses: the site sits on the inbound path for two-wheel couriers who live in Boyle Heights (7th St bridge), Lincoln Heights and South Central (Central Ave/Olympic) - the actual residences of DTLA's two-wheel workforce - so a commute-path design (early-morning hours, secure indoor parking) could partly recover reach.
objections.suggested_value_or_fix: reachable_share lo 0.25 / base 0.38 / hi 0.5; model it by business line (sales 0.5, subscription/swap 0.3) rather than one number.
objections.effect_on_output: SAM_people_hub -20-25% on top of the two-wheel and weekly-people corrections -> ~350-450 people.

objections.claim: Every prior for courier-vehicle subscription in LA is negative, and the SF comparator had advantages the Ceres hub will not have. SOM of 100 by month 12 and 200 by month 24 is roughly 2x what the evidence supports.
objections.evidence: Zoomo - VC-backed, $20/week Uber Eats rider plan, DoorDash/Uber partnerships - operated in LA and retreated to NYC (every ridezoomo.com/us page is now 'Zoomo NYC'); Whizz chose NYC, SF, DC, Philadelphia, Chicago and Jersey City and skipped LA. DoorDash+Whizz's platform-marketed Chicago program converted 'more than 150' car Dashers city-wide in ~9 months in a 2.7M city. HMP SF: 600-1,000 vehicles in ~25 months with a founder on site, walk-in traffic, a seeded referral network and a 72% two-wheel DoorDash share; LA Ceres has none of these and a ~40% two-wheel courier share. The binding constraint is price: a compliant 49cc gas scooter is $899 new; HMP-class e-mopeds are $3-5k plus a battery plan. On the positive side HMP's moped-class product (lane-split capable, 2-5 mi legs) fits LA better than Zoomo/Whizz e-bikes did, so the LA-specific failure of e-bike subscriptions is not a perfect analogue.
objections.suggested_value_or_fix: penetration_m12 0.04-0.06 (base 0.05), penetration_m24 0.10-0.15 (base 0.12); la_maturity_vs_sf 0.5-0.7. With SAM ~400-450: SOM M12 ~20-30 two-wheel + ~15-25 car converts = ~35-50; SOM M24 ~50-65 + ~30-45 = ~80-110.

objections.target: 24-month demand trajectory for two-wheel couriers in exactly these zones (no parameter - missing structural factor)
objections.claim: Sidewalk delivery robots are an LA-born phenomenon concentrated in the model's own zones and they take precisely the sub-1.5-mile orders that bike-mode couriers live on. The model has no term for this, and it bites hardest in the M12-M24 window the SOM is built on.
objections.evidence: LA Times (syndicated 2025-07-25): Coco operates 'more than 1,000 robots' across Santa Monica, Venice, West LA, Westwood, Mid-City, WeHo, Hollywood, Echo Park, Silver Lake, downtown, Koreatown and the USC area, 'targeting 10,000 robots in production next year'; DoorDash separately launched robot delivery in Los Angeles (2025). If each robot completes 5-10 deliveries/day and ~30% of the fleet works DTLA/Koreatown/USC, that is 1,500-3,000 deliveries/day out of the zone's ~16,000 modeled daily app orders (10-20%), all from the short-hop segment that is maybe 40% of zone orders - i.e., 25-45% of the two-wheel courier's order pool. At 10,000 robots the displacement exceeds the zone's entire short-order volume.
objections.suggested_value_or_fix: Add a robot-displacement parameter on zone two-wheel demand: 0.85-0.95 at M12, 0.7-0.9 at M24; hold the two-wheel courier count flat rather than growing it with DoorDash's national '4x faster' trend.

objections.target: zone_order_intensity_vs_county (1.15) and restaurants_target_zone as the allocation key
objections.claim: Restaurant-share allocation is the right key (couriers commute in; orders originate where restaurants are), but DTLA's DPH count is padded with facilities that never appear on an app, and DTLA office lunch is half its pre-2020 size, so the net intensity uplift is ~1.0-1.1, not 1.15.
objections.evidence: DTLA DPH 910 vs NAICS 7225 690 (+32%): the gap is Crypto.com Arena/LA Live concessions, Convention Center, hotel kitchens, ~40 Grand Central Market stalls permitted individually, Fashion District food stalls, Skid Row mission kitchens - none of them app merchants. CBRE Q3 2025: DTLA office vacancy 33.3%, availability 36.8%; Bisnow/CoStar: buildings 'about half as occupied as before the pandemic' despite the state RTO order for ~100k state workers (DTLA has ~150k public-sector jobs). Offsets: Koreatown late-night is a genuine hotspot (Korea Daily: one Korean restaurant ran 3,037 Uber Eats orders in 8 months = ~12.5/day on one app), USC's ~45k students, and orders exported from Ktown/DTLA kitchens to Silver Lake/Echo Park/Mid-City/South LA. Smell test on the model's own number: 16,000 orders/day in the zone = 0.35 orders/resident/week, i.e., NYC-citywide per-capita intensity (0.33) inside a 319k-resident zone - defensible only because of daytime population and export, so 1.15 on top is double-counting.
objections.suggested_value_or_fix: zone_order_intensity_vs_county lo 0.85 / base 1.05 / hi 1.25; or deflate DTLA's restaurant count by ~12-15% for non-app facilities and keep 1.15.
objections.effect_on_output: DAILY_zone all modes ~1,980 -> ~1,800 (-8-10%). This is the main component of the 0.9 all-modes factor.

objections.claim: The P10-P90 band of +/-18% is false precision. The label question alone moves M5 by 3x, the two-wheel courier share is uncertain by +/-30%, and orders/courier, weekly/daily and intensity are correlated (a casual-heavy market has low orders/courier AND low daily/weekly), which the independent-triangle MC ignores.
objections.evidence: model_output.txt: M5_vs_M123_county_two_wheel ranges 0.72-1.28 (P10-P90) while BLEND_zone_two_wheel_daily is reported at 799-1,200; scenario columns span 685-6,164 for M1_zone (9x) yet the MC band is 1.7x. NYC DCWP-derived parameters (0.5 quarterly-to-weekly, 39-45 deliveries/week) are all from the same career-courier regime; using them as independent draws understates joint uncertainty.
objections.suggested_value_or_fix: Report conservative/base/aggressive scenarios only, or impose correlations (rho ~0.5 between orders_per_courier_day, weekly_to_daily, quarterly_to_weekly) and a discrete label-boundary switch.
objections.effect_on_output: No change to the base; the credible band on zone two-wheel should read roughly 500-1,600, not 800-1,200.

objections.target: la_deliveries_per_courier_week (22) / orders_per_courier_day (9) - the counter-risk to this critique
objections.claim: For balance: the one route by which the all-modes headline could be biased LOW is courier productivity. 22 deliveries/week implies ~11-14 hours/week on app for the average weekly-active LA courier, above DoorDash's stated CA average of ~6 hours/week on delivery. If the true blend is ~15/week, county weekly-active is ~90k and daily-active ~36k, and the zone all-modes figure is ~1.4x higher.
objections.evidence: DoorDash Prop 22 post (2024-05-17): 'California Dashers spent an average of roughly six hours per week on delivery' (active time; online time perhaps 9-10 hrs). Seattle OLS: 12.7 completed offers per engaged account-week, 7.3 engaged hours. Multi-apping (NYC: 1.8 accounts per person) raises per-person counts back toward 15-20.
objections.suggested_value_or_fix: Widen la_deliveries_per_courier_week to lo 28 / base 18 / hi 13. This does not rescue the two-wheel or e-moped numbers - it would add casual car couriers, not riders.
objections.effect_on_output: Possible +20-40% on DAILY_zone all modes and DAILY_county; ~0 on two-wheel and SAM.

objections.target: evidence_mode_split.json synthesis on Koreatown (Korean-language sources used to infer Ktown courier mode)
objections.claim: The Korean-community evidence (heykorean '차로 배달', Radio Korea 부업 Q&A, absence of 오토바이 rider ads) characterizes Korean side-hustlers, who are a small minority of the couriers picking up at Koreatown restaurants. Koreatown is ~53% Latino / ~30% Asian; the 7pm pickup line at a KBBQ is mostly Latino and Black car couriers plus a Latino minority on gas mopeds and e-bikes. The absence of a Seoul-style employed-rider culture is true but is the wrong population for setting the app-courier mode split. Separately, JQS Delivery (since 2010, car/van) and RushOrder capture a slice of Korean-restaurant orders outside the apps, trimming Ktown's app order volume by perhaps 10-15%.
objections.evidence: evidence ids 19-24 in evidence_mode_split.json; Koreatown demographics (ACS: majority Hispanic, ~one-third Asian); Korea Daily 2025-04-03 shows Korean restaurants do run substantial Uber Eats volume, with no mode data.
objections.suggested_value_or_fix: Do not let Korean-language sources move the Koreatown two-wheel share; use an intercept count (see what_would_settle_it). Apply a 0.85-0.9 app-share factor to Koreatown's Korean-restaurant subset if JQS/RushOrder volume matters.
objections.effect_on_output: Negligible on totals (<3%); affects narrative credibility of the Koreatown section.

things_the_model_got_right: The all-modes headline (~2,000 daily-active in the zone) passes the peak-hour smell test: ~60% online at 7pm = ~1,190 couriers across 1,962 DPH restaurants = 0.61 concurrent per restaurant (~0.8 per app-active restaurant), ~2,080 pickups/hour = ~1.06 per restaurant-hour; in Koreatown that is ~370 couriers online in 2.4 sq mi, one per ~4 acres, roughly one per block face - consistent with what a walk down 6th St from Vermont to Western shows on a Friday at 7pm (a handful of pickups per block, 5-10/hour at a busy KBBQ, one every hour or two at the median place). NYC's 49k daily-active / 23k restaurants = 2.1 per restaurant, so the zone is modeled at ~48% of NYC citywide density and perhaps 25-30% of Midtown - the right order.

Allocating by restaurant count rather than resident population is correct: couriers commute in (Seattle: 74.7% live outside city limits; DTLA's two-wheel riders live in Boyle Heights, Lincoln Heights, Pico-Union, South Central), and orders originate where the kitchens are.

Treating DoorDash's 49% as a DELIVERY share and converting to a smaller COURIER share is the right direction; Uber Eats LA being more car-heavy (rideshare pool, <50cc scooter rule) is correctly flagged.

The 3-mile radius (2,021 restaurants / 452k residents) and the five-NC zone (1,962 / 319k) are nearly the same object, so the hub catchment is framed correctly; the 1.5-mile radius (975 restaurants) is the honest core.
car_convertible_share 2-10% is realistic; the model correctly cites the Chicago DoorDash+Whizz program at 'more than 150' conversions citywide.

Flagging that DTLA DPH counts include hotel/stadium/institutional kitchens, that LA has no courier rental fleet (Whizz absent), and that 768 Ceres is on the Skid Row edge after dark - the model saw the issues even where it under-weighted them.

The county-level cross-check across M1/M2/M3 (~62k weekly, ~25k daily; 0.63% of residents weekly-active vs NYC 0.72%) is internally coherent and plausible for a market with ~43% of NYC's per-capita order intensity and a casual-majority courier base.
weekly_to_daily 0.4 is right for the car-courier majority (DoorDash CA ~6 hrs/week) - the error is applying it to two-wheelers.
la_maturity_vs_sf_at_m24 < 1.0 and the note that SF's growth came from founder presence, walk-in and referral network is exactly the right lens; it just needs to be applied harder at M12.
what_would_settle_it: A three-evening intercept count (Thu-Sat, 6:30-8:30pm) at five pickup points: 7th/Figueroa or Grand Central Market (DTLA), 1st/Central (Little Tokyo), 6th/Western or Wilshire/Normandie (Koreatown), Alvarado/6th (Westlake), Figueroa/Jefferson (USC). Tally every courier by mode: car / gas scooter or motorcycle / e-bike or e-moto / standing e-scooter / e-moped / pedal / on foot. n=300-500 gives the zone mode split to +/-5 points and directly tests 53% two-wheel and 65% electric. Cost: one person, three evenings.

Ask DoorDash press or policy what geography 'Los Angeles, CA' denotes in the 2026 Two-Wheeled Progress Report (city limits, DoorDash submarket, or metro) and whether 'two-wheel miles traveled' counts miles while online without an active delivery. This alone decides whether M5 corroborates or contradicts M1-M3 and whether the 0.6 NYC calibration is legitimate.

A Dasher-app check inside the zone: which dash types LA offers (Bike / Scooter / Motorcycle?), whether Scooter mode requires the vehicle background check in LA, and whether short-order bike zones exist at 768 Ceres's starting point. Also whether DoorDash has ever sent 'car-speed in bike mode' warnings in LA - a proxy for how much of the 49% is car.

20-30 structured interviews with two-wheel couriers at the intercept points: home ZIP, days/week, vehicle type and price paid, license status, where they charge/fuel, willingness to ride to 7th/Ceres for a swap or service, and price ceiling for an e-moped plus battery plan. This settles weekly_to_daily for two-wheelers, reachable_share, and the gas-vs-electric economics.
DMV motorized-scooter/moped registration counts by ZIP (90005-90007, 90010-90021, 90057) and Uber/DoorDash 'scooter' sign-up availability - the only public quantification of the gas fleet.
Zoomo LA's peak subscriber count (2021-2023) and the reason it consolidated to NYC - the closest thing to a natural experiment for an LA courier-vehicle hub SOM; one call to former Zoomo US staff.
Coco's deliveries per robot-day and neighborhood coverage map for DTLA/Koreatown/USC, to size short-hop displacement over the M12-M24 window.

A Gridwise or Solo LA data cut of delivery users by vehicle type and hours/week, which would replace three ESTIMATE parameters (two_wheel_delivery_to_courier_share, weekly_to_daily_active for two-wheelers, la_deliveries_per_courier_week) with data.
